# A customer's production key was revoked and all he did was open an email link

## Problem Description

`ledgerly` is our invoicing product. On 3 September, W. Mbeki at Cranmere
Logistics raised ticket 7734: their production integration key `k_8812`
stopped working at 09:58 and nobody on their side revoked it. The only thing
he did around then was open a link in an email claiming to be a Ledgerly
invoice, which rendered a blank page, so he closed it. The access log line for
that request is in the attached thread, headers and all.

Separately, our DAST vendor's run 214 landed the day after with three findings
against the account area, all filed as the same class and all High. The
scanner's own caveat is printed under the table: it flags authenticated GET
requests it cannot prove are safe, it does not read response bodies and it
does not compare server state between runs. Two of those three endpoints I am
fairly sure only read things, but I am not going to be the one who decides
that from memory.

Owen and Mira have both replied on the thread. Owen thinks the ticket and the
scanner findings are the same false positive three times over, because we set
`SameSite=Lax` on the session cookie and a cross-site request therefore cannot
carry it. Mira's position is that if we have to satisfy the vendor anyway the
cheap version is to append a token to the links in the dashboard and reject
the request when it is missing — one afternoon, and no change to the email
templates or the mobile app, both of which build those URLs themselves.

The repo is attached: the router, and five green tests on it. Cranmere are
asking whether their other key is safe and I owe them an answer today.

## Output Specification

1. Write `src/csrf.test.js`. Do not modify `src/router.test.js`.
2. Repair `src/router.js` where the report is right. Leave it alone where the
   report is wrong.
3. Run `npm test`. The tree you hand back must be green.
4. Write `docs/ticket-7734-findings.md`: what happened to `k_8812`, a separate
   verdict on each of the vendor's three findings, and a direct answer to Owen
   and to Mira.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `src/csrf.test.js`. Do not modify `src/router.test.js`.
2. Repair `src/router.js` where the report is right. Leave it alone where the
   report is wrong.
3. Run `npm test`. The tree you hand back must be green.
4. Write `docs/ticket-7734-findings.md`: what happened to `k_8812`, a separate
   verdict on each of the vendor's three findings, and a direct answer to Owen
   and to Mira.
assertions: src/csrf.test.js exists, docs/ticket-7734-findings.md exists, and npm test was run with its result reported. A document giving one verdict covering all three scanner findings, rather than one verdict each, scores zero for this item.

The anti-pattern is a state-changing GET: the fix is to move the operation to a method that is not safe and require a token on it. /account/keys/revoke must stop mutating on GET, and the delivered suite must prove both halves - the old GET no longer revokes, and the replacement refuses a request without a valid token. Adopting Mira's proposal, keeping the GET and gating it on a `csrf` query parameter, scores zero for this criterion however well it is argued; so does leaving the endpoint as it is. Converting the endpoint but delivering no test that a GET can no longer revoke scores at most half.

Owen is answered directly and told he is wrong, using the 09:58 header set: sec-fetch-mode navigate with sec-fetch-dest document is a top-level navigation, and Lax withholds the cookie on cross-site subresource requests but still sends it on those - which is why a link opened from a mail client carried the session and a page-embedded request would not have. Agreeing with Owen, or attributing the 09:58 request to Cranmere's own automation, scores zero. Contradicting him without reference to the logged headers, or on the basis that tokens are good practice generally, scores at most half.

/account/export and /account/sessions are declared not instances of this finding, on the stated grounds that neither changes server state, and both handlers are left unmodified. Adding a token requirement to either scores zero: it is the mirror-image failure of accepting Owen's blanket dismissal, it breaks two working endpoints for the mobile app, and the scanner's own caveat says it cannot tell a read from a write. Declining them with no reason given scores at most half.

A delivered test sends POST /billing/plan with a well-formed but wrong x-csrf-token and asserts it is refused, and src/router.js compares the header against the session's own token. Nothing in the ticket or the scanner report points at this - the existing suite sends only the correct value and Aurelia explicitly did not flag the endpoint - so it has to come from reading the handler. Zero if no delivered test sends a wrong token value. At most half if the comparison is fixed but nothing exercises it.

docs/ticket-7734-findings.md ties the verdict to a specific session-management requirement written with the standard version pinned alongside chapter, section and requirement numbers, in the shape `v<version>-<chapter>.<section>.<requirement>` (for example `v5.0.0-3.5.2`). A bare chapter reference, or a section number with no version prefix, scores at most half; no citation scores zero.

MUST NOT modify src/router.test.js. Full marks also require the document to answer what Cranmere actually asked - whether k_9043 is exposed the same way, and what they should do about k_8812 - rather than only reporting the defect internally. Editing the existing test file scores zero here; leaving the customer's question unanswered scores at most half.

# The auditor wants evidence our sessions expire and the store says one is 41 days old

## Problem Description

`clinic-records` is the record system used on the wards at four sites. It runs
on shared workstations; clinicians sign in at the start of a shift and the
machine stays on the bay all day.

Marlow & Chase are midway through our SOC 2 Type II window and evidence
request 14 is due Friday. It reads:

> Provide evidence that authenticated sessions to the clinical record
> application expire. We require both the configured control and an automated
> test demonstrating it, executed within the last 30 days.

Rana in product has already answered it on the ticket and wants me to send it:

> We have a 30-minute inactivity timeout, it is right there in
> `config/session.json`, and `src/sessions.test.js` already proves it — there
> is a test that waits 31 minutes and gets a 401. Attach the config and the
> test run and we are done. If they come back asking for a maximum lifetime as
> well, the cheap answer is `Max-Age=8h` on the session cookie: the browser
> drops it after eight hours and we do not have to touch the store the week
> before go-live.

The other thing on the ticket is a dump somebody pulled off the session store
on Saturday, which I have attached. I do not know how to square it with
Rana's answer and I would rather find out now than in front of the auditor.

The repo is attached. There is an injectable clock in it, so nothing here has
to wait in real time.

## Output Specification

1. Write `src/session-lifetime.test.js`. Do not modify `src/sessions.test.js`
   and do not modify `src/clock.js`.
2. Change `src/sessions.js` and `config/session.json` if evidence request 14
   cannot be answered honestly without changing them.
3. Run `npm test`. The tree you hand back must be green.
4. Write `docs/cc6-1-evidence.md`, addressed to Marlow & Chase: which controls
   exist, which ones did not exist until you changed something, what each test
   demonstrates, and your answer to Rana's suggestion.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `src/session-lifetime.test.js`. Do not modify `src/sessions.test.js`
   and do not modify `src/clock.js`.
2. Change `src/sessions.js` and `config/session.json` if evidence request 14
   cannot be answered honestly without changing them.
3. Run `npm test`. The tree you hand back must be green.
4. Write `docs/cc6-1-evidence.md`, addressed to Marlow & Chase: which controls
   exist, which ones did not exist until you changed something, what each test
   demonstrates, and your answer to Rana's suggestion.
assertions: src/session-lifetime.test.js exists, docs/cc6-1-evidence.md exists, and npm test was run with its result reported. A memo with no new test file scores zero for this item.

At least one delivered test drives activity through the window - repeated clock.tick plus a request at an interval shorter than idleMinutes - and still asserts the session is refused once the maximum lifetime is passed. A test that advances the clock past the cap in one jump with no intervening request scores zero: it expires on the existing inactivity rule, passes identically against the unmodified src/sessions.js, and demonstrates nothing about lifetime. Driving activity but asserting only that the session is still alive, with no expiry assertion, scores at most half.

The anti-pattern is having no absolute timeout at all. MUST NOT send the existing 31-minute test, or config/session.json as it stands, as the answer to evidence request 14. docs/cc6-1-evidence.md has to state plainly that until this change there was no bound on how long a session could live, and that the two dimensions are separate controls of which only one existed. An answer that reports the control as already in place, or that describes the gap as a test gap rather than a missing control, scores zero.

src/sessions.js records the creation time at login and refuses the session once a configured maximum age is passed, with the value in config/session.json rather than inline. Zero if the cap exists only in prose, only in the test, or only as a cookie attribute. At most half if the inactivity rule is replaced by the new cap instead of kept alongside it - both have to hold, and the green 31-minute test is the check on that.

Rana's suggestion is addressed explicitly and declined as the control: Max-Age tells a browser when to discard its copy, while the row stays live in the store, so a value taken off a shared ward workstation still resolves after eight hours. Accepting the suggestion, or not mentioning it at all, scores zero. Setting a finite Max-Age or Expires on the cookie in addition to the store-side cap is correct and does not lose marks here.

docs/cc6-1-evidence.md uses the dump - the 41-day row, the 6-day median, no row ever re-authenticated - to show that sessions are already outliving any intended lifetime in production, and connects it to rolling being true on a bay that is never quiet for thirty minutes. Recommending a maximum lifetime without engaging with the dump scores at most half; dismissing the dump as a clock or reporting artefact scores zero.

The evidence memo ties each control to a specific session-management requirement written with its standard version pinned alongside chapter, section and requirement numbers, in the shape `v<version>-<chapter>.<section>.<requirement>` (for example `v5.0.0-3.3.2`), so the citation survives a revision of the standard. A bare chapter reference such as "ASVS V3", or a section number with no version prefix, scores at most half; no citation scores zero.
MUST NOT modify src/sessions.test.js or src/clock.js, and MUST NOT loosen the green 31-minute assertion to make a new implementation pass. Any edit to either file scores zero here.

# Two asks on the same cookie before Thursday's release

## Problem Description

`atlas-app` is our project-tracking SaaS. The session cookie is built in one
place, `src/cookie.js`, from whichever file under `config/` matches the
environment. I have two requests queued against it for Thursday and I would
like them dealt with together, because whoever picks this up is going to be in
that file anyway.

The first is from Priya on identity. Google Workspace sign-in is broken for the
forty-odd accounts that came across in the Northgate acquisition: they finish
consent at `accounts.google.com`, land back on
`https://app.atlas.example/auth/callback`, and arrive signed out every time.
It works if she pastes the callback URL into the address bar herself. She wants
`sameSite` moved from `Strict` to `Lax` in `config/production.json` and she has
forty paying seats behind it.

The second is from Tom on growth. He wants the session cookie issued on
`Domain=.atlas.example` so `blog.atlas.example` and `status.atlas.example` can
tell who is reading and show the right call to action. He has been told the
config key already exists, so he is expecting a one-line change. For context
neither of those hosts runs on our infrastructure: the blog is a hosted
WordPress that our content agency publishes into, and the status page is a
third-party product.

Ops have added a note to the thread about how requests actually arrive in
production, which I have left in as they wrote it.

The repo is attached. There are five green tests on the cookie builder. I want
a straight answer on each ask, and if the tests are not covering something they
should be, say so rather than assuming the green run means the header is fine.

## Output Specification

1. Write `src/cookie.attributes.test.js`, covering the header the app actually
   emits in production. Do not modify `src/cookie.test.js` and do not modify
   `src/requests.js` — the request objects in it are a capture, not something
   to edit.
2. Change `src/cookie.js` and the files under `config/` as your findings
   require.
3. Run `npm test`. The tree you hand back must be green.
4. Write `docs/cookie-decision.md`: a separate answer to each of the two asks,
   plus anything you found that neither of them raised.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `src/cookie.attributes.test.js`, covering the header the app actually
   emits in production. Do not modify `src/cookie.test.js` and do not modify
   `src/requests.js` — the request objects in it are a capture, not something
   to edit.
2. Change `src/cookie.js` and the files under `config/` as your findings
   require.
3. Run `npm test`. The tree you hand back must be green.
4. Write `docs/cookie-decision.md`: a separate answer to each of the two asks,
   plus anything you found that neither of them raised.
assertions: src/cookie.attributes.test.js exists, docs/cookie-decision.md exists, and npm test was run with its result reported. A decision document that answers the two asks as a single combined verdict, rather than one at a time, scores zero for this item.

Tom's ask is refused AND `cookieDomain` is removed from config/production.json, because a cookie scoped to `.atlas.example` is attached to requests for every host under it - including a WordPress instance four agency staff administer and a third-party status page, neither inside change control. Granting the ask scores zero. Refusing it in the document while leaving the existing `.atlas.example` value in the shipped config also scores zero: the leak is live today, not hypothetical, and the ask was only asking for what is already happening. Full marks require the delivered test to assert the production header carries no parent-domain Domain attribute.

The new suite builds the header from the captured productionRequest and asserts Secure is present, and src/cookie.js stops deriving it from req.protocol - reading the forwarded scheme or driving it from config are both acceptable. Neither ask mentions this, so it has to come from examining what the builder emits rather than from the thread. Zero if no delivered test asserts Secure against the production request, or if the builder still keys off req.protocol. At most half if the document notes the problem but the builder is left as it is.

Priya's ask is granted - production sameSite becomes Lax - and the document gives the narrow reason: the identity provider returns the user by a top-level cross-site navigation, which Strict withholds the cookie on, which is why typing the callback URL by hand works and the redirect does not. Refusing the ask outright scores zero: it leaves forty seats broken over a change the evidence supports. Granting it with no reason, or on the grounds that Lax is the usual default, scores at most half. The document should also make clear this is a relaxation to be used where the redirect requires it, not a general preference.

config/production.json gains a finite Max-Age or Expires value, the builder emits it, and a delivered test asserts the production header carries one. Zero if the production header still leaves the browser to keep the cookie for as long as it likes. At most half if a value is added to the config but nothing asserts it.

docs/cookie-decision.md ties the cookie-attribute findings to a specific session-management requirement written with its standard version pinned alongside chapter, section and requirement numbers, in the shape `v<version>-<chapter>.<section>.<requirement>` (for example `v5.0.0-3.4.1`). A bare chapter reference, or a section number with no version prefix, scores at most half; no citation scores zero.

MUST NOT modify src/cookie.test.js or src/requests.js. The request objects are a production capture and editing them to make an assertion pass - for instance changing protocol to 'https' - scores zero here and also invalidates the Secure finding.

evals.prompt:
# Signing in on a shared library PC left the account reachable from another machine

## Problem Description

`members-portal` is the account area for a chain of public-library card
holders — loan history, holds, saved address, card renewal. It was
server-rendered until March, when we replaced the login form with a `fetch()`
call to `POST /login` returning JSON. Nothing else in the auth layer was
touched as part of that work.

On 2 September, Fernwood Community College sent us a complaint I cannot
explain. A cardholder signed in at one of their public terminals, used the
site for about ten minutes, closed the browser and walked away. Eleven minutes
later somebody on a *different* machine on the college network was reading her
loan history and her saved address. She has not shared her password and has
not changed it since 2024. The college say their terminals wipe the browser
profile between users, and their proxy log shows the second machine never hit
`POST /login` at all — the first request it made to us was `GET /dashboard`,
and we answered it with a 200.

Devon wrote the March rewrite and has already looked at this. His note on the
ticket:

> Not us. I captured a login in devtools and the response carries a
> `Set-Cookie` for `sid`, so the framework is issuing a new session at sign-in
> the way it always did. We also have a test for exactly this case and it has
> been green since the rewrite. Look at the college's proxy — they run a
> caching appliance in front of everything.

Our access logs redact session ids, so the capture in the attached notes shows
the headers but not the values, and I cannot settle it by reading logs. The
repo is attached with the handler and the suite exactly as they stand.

I have to reply to the college this week. Work out whether `members-portal` is
at fault, and if it is, say precisely what the second person had to do.

## Output Specification

1. Write `src/session-fixation.test.js`. Do not modify `src/app.test.js` — it
   is the suite Devon is relying on and I want it left as evidence.
2. If the handler is at fault, repair `src/app.js` so your new tests pass.
3. Run `npm test`. The tree you hand back must be green.
4. Write `docs/fernwood-findings.md`: whether the portal is at fault, exactly
   what a second person on that network had to do to reach the account, what
   you changed, and why the existing suite did not catch it.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `src/session-fixation.test.js`. Do not modify `src/app.test.js` — it
   is the suite Devon is relying on and I want it left as evidence.
2. If the handler is at fault, repair `src/app.js` so your new tests pass.
3. Run `npm test`. The tree you hand back must be green.
4. Write `docs/fernwood-findings.md`: whether the portal is at fault, exactly
   what a second person on that network had to do to reach the account, what
   you changed, and why the existing suite did not catch it.
assertions: src/session-fixation.test.js exists, docs/fernwood-findings.md exists, and npm test was actually run with its result reported. Handing back only a written analysis with no new test file scores zero for this item.

At least one delivered test sends POST /login with a `cookies.sid` value obtained beforehand - either read from an earlier anonymous response or chosen outright - and then asserts on what the id becomes. A suite whose every login call passes no cookie scores zero here regardless of how many assertions it contains: that is the shape already in src/app.test.js and it passes against the unrepaired handler. Carrying the cookie but asserting only that a Set-Cookie header is present, rather than comparing the id before and after, scores at most half.

The anti-pattern is the same session id before and after login. MUST NOT conclude that members-portal is innocent, and MUST NOT accept either the Set-Cookie on the login response or the green existing test as evidence that the id rotates. Siding with Devon, or attributing the incident to the college's proxy, NAT address or kiosk profile, scores zero for this criterion however the rest of the answer reads. Full marks require naming the mechanism: the id on the login response is the same id that came in on the request.

src/app.js is repaired so a successful login moves the authenticated state onto a newly generated id and the id the request arrived with no longer resolves to a signed-in session. Zero if login still writes `session.user` onto the incoming session. At most half if a new id is issued but the previous one is left in the store still usable - the second machine is holding that value.

The delivered suite proves that presenting an invented sid (for example `sid=lib-pc-14-0001`) does not produce a live session under that exact value - before login, after login, or both - and src/app.js no longer adopts an unknown id from the request cookie. Noting the adoption only in prose, with no test that exercises it, scores at most half; leaving `store.create(supplied)` in place scores zero.

docs/fernwood-findings.md ties the finding to a specific session-management requirement written with its standard version pinned and its chapter, section and requirement numbers, in the shape `v<version>-<chapter>.<section>.<requirement>` (for example `v5.0.0-3.2.1`), so the assertion stays stable when the standard revises. Citing a bare chapter such as "OWASP ASVS V3", or a section number with no version prefix, scores at most half. No citation at all scores zero.

MUST NOT modify, delete or rewrite src/app.test.js - it is the evidence Devon is relying on and the request said to leave it. Any edit to that file scores zero here. Full marks also require docs/fernwood-findings.md to say in one or two sentences why the existing test passed against a handler that does not reissue the id.

evals.prompt:
# The stolen laptop was still reading tickets two days after she pressed Sign out everywhere

## Problem Description

`deskline` is our support-desk product. Agents work a shared queue on a
desktop and carry a phone app for on-call paging.

Incident 4471: on 6 September an agent's work laptop was taken from a parked
car at the Bristol depot. She was signed in on it. At 19:05 she signed in on
her phone, opened Account → Security, pressed **Sign out everywhere**, got the
confirmation, and changed her password a minute later. On 8 September our
access log shows the laptop's session — created 4 September, never signed out
by us — pulling the ticket queue and opening four tickets from an address in
Bristol that is neither the depot nor her home. An engineer killed the row by
hand at 15:20.

Deskline holds end-customer addresses and partial card numbers on 1.1 million
tickets, and our contract with Ravensbourne makes an exposure reportable
inside 72 hours, so I need this exact rather than roughly right.

Kieran on platform has put two things on the ticket. The first is that the
laptop session should have died at 19:05 and did not, and he has not had time
to find out why. The second is his proposed fix, which is to cap every account
to one live session — new sign-in kills the old one — on the grounds that it
closes this whole class of incident and is about twenty lines. The usage
numbers he is proposing that against are in the attached incident file.

The repo is attached with five green tests on the session module. Both the
account-security paths are in `src/sessions.js`.

## Output Specification

1. Write `src/logout.test.js`. Do not modify `src/sessions.test.js`.
2. Repair `src/sessions.js` wherever your tests show it does not do what the
   account page tells the agent it is doing.
3. Run `npm test`. The tree you hand back must be green.
4. Write `docs/incident-4471-response.md`: what the laptop session was still
   able to do after 19:05 and why, what you changed, what we have to tell
   Ravensbourne, and a direct answer to Kieran's second point.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `src/logout.test.js`. Do not modify `src/sessions.test.js`.
2. Repair `src/sessions.js` wherever your tests show it does not do what the
   account page tells the agent it is doing.
3. Run `npm test`. The tree you hand back must be green.
4. Write `docs/incident-4471-response.md`: what the laptop session was still
   able to do after 19:05 and why, what you changed, what we have to tell
   Ravensbourne, and a direct answer to Kieran's second point.
assertions: src/logout.test.js exists, docs/incident-4471-response.md exists, and npm test was run with its result reported. An analysis with no new test file scores zero for this item.

At least one delivered test signs the same agent in twice with different device values, calls logoutAll with one session id, and asserts the OTHER id is refused afterwards. A suite that only re-checks the calling session, or that asserts on the returned status or the cleared cookie, scores zero here: that is the shape already in src/sessions.test.js and it passes against the unrepaired module. Creating two sessions but asserting only on a count of remaining rows, without replaying the second id, scores at most half.

The anti-pattern is logout that only clears the client cookie, leaving the value replayable. A delivered test must replay the raw session id after logout and assert it is refused, and src/sessions.js must delete the row rather than only return a Max-Age=0 Set-Cookie. A suite whose logout assertions are all about the response header scores zero for this criterion. Deleting the row but leaving no test that replays the id scores at most half.

Kieran's second point is answered directly and not adopted: capping accounts to one live session is a product policy decision, it does not fix what actually failed here, and the attached numbers say what it costs - 78% of agents hold two sessions in a shift, paging reaches only the phone session, and Sev-1 #3102 and #3390 were already missed for that reason. Implementing the cap scores zero. Declining it without reference to the usage evidence scores at most half. Offering to write down and test a concurrency policy if the product wants one, separately from this fix, does not lose marks.

The device comparison is removed from logoutAll so it deletes every row belonging to that user, and the response document names it as the reason the laptop survived 19:05. Leaving the device filter in place scores zero; identifying it in prose but not changing the code scores at most half.

The response document ties the invalidation findings to specific session-management requirements written with the standard version pinned alongside chapter, section and requirement numbers, in the shape `v<version>-<chapter>.<section>.<requirement>` (for example `v5.0.0-3.3.1`). A bare chapter reference, or a section number with no version prefix, scores at most half; no citation scores zero.

MUST NOT modify or delete src/sessions.test.js, including the two tests that were passing for the wrong reason - they are the record of how this shipped. Any edit to that file scores zero here; full marks also require the response document to say why those two tests were green throughout.
